context_blurb:
A force is a push or a pull, and forces start things moving, speed them up, slow them down or turn them. Every force has a size, how strong it is, and a direction, the way it acts. Add up the forces on anything, from a sled to a skydiver, and you can tell what it will do next.

Forces come in two kinds. Contact forces act only where two things touch: friction, the rub between surfaces that works against sliding, and the normal force, a surface's push back on whatever rests on it. Gravity and magnetism pull across a gap instead: Earth pulls a falling apple, and a magnet tugs a paper clip, before anything touches. So whether a force acts only where things touch is what sorts it into one kind or the other. Earth's gravity pulls everything straight down, toward the planet's centre.

In a force diagram, every force acting on an object is drawn as an arrow pointing the way the force acts. The arrow's length shows how strong the force is: the longer the arrow, the stronger the force. The arrows stand for forces, not motion, so a book lying still on a table gets two arrows of equal length, gravity's pointing down and the table's pointing up.

Add all the forces together, minding their directions, and you get the net force: forces acting the same way add, opposite forces take away from each other, and the net force points the way of the stronger push or pull. When the net force is zero, the forces are balanced and the motion does not change: a still thing stays still, and a moving thing keeps the same speed in a straight line. When the forces are unbalanced, the motion changes in the direction of the net force.

A brick on a soft mattress makes a dip; on a stone floor it leaves no mark. Yet the brick sits still on both, so on both the surface's push up exactly matches gravity's pull down, and the two normal forces are equal. Stone is squeezed too, far too little to see, and pushes back like a very stiff spring, while the mattress only sinks further before its push matches the load.

A sled resting on flat snow is balanced, the snow pushing up as hard as gravity pulls down. Then a girl pulls it to the right, harder than friction holds it back. With her pull bigger than friction, the net force points right, so the sled starts moving right and speeds up, and it keeps speeding up for as long as she out-pulls friction.

Balanced forces do not mean a thing is still. A car cruising at a steady speed on a level road has balanced forces: since its speed is not changing, the engine's forward force exactly equals the backward push of friction and the air. A bigger forward force would speed it up; a smaller one would slow it.

Air resistance, or drag, is the air's push against anything moving through it, and it grows the faster the thing goes. A girl pedalling hard on a level road speeds up at first. But the air pushes back harder as she speeds up, and once its push matches hers, the forces are balanced and her speed holds steady.

A skydiver falls faster and faster until the air's upward push matches gravity, then drops at a steady speed. Her parachute's wide canopy catches far more air, so the moment it opens, the upward push beats gravity. The net force now points up, against her motion, so she keeps falling, but more slowly. She never rises: as she slows, the air's push weakens until it matches gravity again while she is still moving down, and she drifts down at five to eight metres a second. Films seem to show her shooting up only because the camera, carried by another skydiver, is still falling fast.
